title: Sweet Sixteen
full_review:
"Sweet Sixteen" (Lions Gate) is a poignant tale of a Scottish teen driven to extreme measures to better his own life and the lives of his loved ones. True to his life's work as chronicler and poet of Britain's working classes, director Ken Loach elicits nuanced performances out of his adolescent leads to create an engaging portrait of a boy on the cusp of adulthood, struggling to make sense out of life's sometimes harsh realities.

The story focuses on Liam (Martin Compston), a resourceful lad just shy of his 16th birthday. His jailbird mother, Jean (Michelle Coulter), is doing time on drug-related charges but is due to be released soon. Liam, when not hustling a buck or getting into trouble with his loose-cannon mate, Pinball (William Ruane), dreams of starting life anew with his mum, safe from the reaches of his mean-spirited grandfather (Tommy McKee) and Jean's low-life boyfriend, Stan (Gary McCormack), a sadistic petty drug dealer who routinely strong-arms Liam into helping him ply his trade -- noncompliance resulting in savage beatings.

After some particularly brutal tough love, Liam moves in with his sister, Chantelle (Annmarie Fulton), an overworked single mom barely older than Liam juggling homemaking duties and correspondence courses in the hope of bettering her lot. Though she is sincerely worried about her brother's welfare, her no-nonsense sensibilities and less-than-confident prognosis of their mother's rehabilitation inject an unwelcome dose of reality into Liam's idyllic optimism.

Undeterred, Liam -- audacious as he is desperate -- takes matters into his own hands, literally, by stealing a stash of drugs from Stan and selling them at a profit. When his entrepreneurial moxie catches the eye of a local crime boss (Martin McCardie), Liam finds himself in way over his head. And though the lucrative business arrangement sets him on the yellow brick road to a better life with his mom, it comes at grave cost: his soul.

Though much of what unfolds on the screen is fueled by violence -- both physical and emotional -- the film is an elegiac exploration of the powerful bond between parents and their children. While neither justifying nor glamorizing heinous crimes perpetrated by the young protagonist, Liam's actions are presented as a misguided attempt to create, by any means necessary, that which will give his life meaning and completeness: a family. Liam's rage is a primal scream, an existential self-defense against the despair threatening to destroy his hope of a better life.

And though he destroys lives in the process, viewers should not overlook Liam's wounded humanity. The final haunting image reveals his brokenness -- a boy longing for his mother, willing to forgive her faults, but unable to control the forces keeping them apart. As the filmmaker observes, "Fragility and often a wild courage, even if misplaced, can sit easily side by side."

Chantelle stands in as a positive counterpoint to Liam's recklessness. She does not use society as a convenient scapegoat; she demands accountability for the ill-advised choices Liam and Jean have made. For her, virtue is a matter of hard work and does not suffer behaviorist fools gladly.

This modest film, which may prove daunting to viewers in the early goings due to the actors' heavy Scottish brogues -- necessitating subtitles throughout -- flowers beautifully and offers moments of genuine pathos without airbrushed sentimentality or a pat resolution.

Subtitles.

Due to much rough language, as well as profanities, recurring drug abuse and some instances of violence, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
